forces.title: Softening Global Metal Prices Impact Irish Metals Sector
forces.description: The metals sector in Ireland is facing headwinds from softer global metal prices, which require businesses to manage purchasing decisions carefully. This market condition directly affects the revenue and profitability of Irish metals firms, especially if they cannot effectively pass on cost increases to customers. Maintaining strong cash conversion and inventory discipline becomes crucial as market conditions normalize from recent highs.

forces.title: Persistent Cost Pressures Challenge Irish Metals Profitability
forces.description: Irish metals businesses are experiencing persistent raw material and labor cost pressures, which are weighing on margins. This necessitates careful assessment of how much cost inflation can be realistically passed on to customers without damaging relationships. The challenge is particularly acute for automotive suppliers, where raw materials like steel remain volatile and operators often work on slim margins, demanding vigilance and effective cost management strategies.

forces.title: International Trade Policy and Tariff Uncertainty for Irish Metals
forces.description: Uncertainty surrounding international trade policies and tariffs poses a significant risk for the Irish metals sector. This external factor can impact import/export costs and competitive dynamics, requiring firms to monitor developments closely. Managing tariff exposure, especially for export-focused firms, and reviewing pricing strategies, hedging arrangements, and customer contract terms are vital to mitigate potential margin erosion if tariffs cannot be fully passed on.

forces.title: CBAM Drives Carbon Costs for Imported Metals into Europe
forces.description: The EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) has converted embedded emissions in imported goods, such as steel, into direct costs since January 2026. This fundamentally changes the cost structure for EU importers, effectively increasing landed costs and thereby impacting margins. These higher carbon-related costs cascade through the value chain, raising expenses for downstream industries and reinforcing the strategic importance of tracking and verifying emissions data.
forces.source_title: CBAM: How companies can build from compliance to value creation

forces.title: Verified Emissions Data Offers Significant CBAM Cost Reduction
forces.description: Companies can substantially reduce their CBAM costs, potentially by 30% to 85% per metric ton, by using verified 'real emissions' data instead of relying on conservative default values. This creates a powerful incentive for EU importers and their non-EU suppliers to invest in robust monitoring, reporting, and verification (MRV) systems. Early movers can gain a competitive advantage by providing credible product-level emissions data, enabling customers to minimize their carbon-related expenses and optimize sourcing decisions.
forces.source_title: CBAM: How companies can build from compliance to value creation

forces.title: European Steel Sector Shifts to Lower-Carbon Production Routes
forces.description: The European steel industry is undergoing a significant structural shift towards electric arc furnace (EAF) and direct reduced iron-electric arc furnace (DRI-EAF) technologies, moving away from traditional blast furnace–basic oxygen furnace (BF-BOF) methods. This transition, particularly in countries like Germany and Sweden, is driven by environmental concerns and policies aimed at reducing carbon footprints, despite higher energy costs. Over 17 EAF/DRI-EAF plants are planned in Europe to produce 40-50 million tons of low-carbon steel by 2030.
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: High Energy Costs Impair European Green Steel Competitiveness
forces.description: Structurally high natural gas and electricity prices in Europe are a major headwind for the region's DRI-EAF steel production, which is crucial for decarbonization. European DRI-EAF levelized costs are 45-50% higher than in the Middle East, with gas costs 2-5 times higher and electricity costs up to double. This significant energy cost disadvantage makes it challenging for European low-carbon steel to compete globally, even with policy support, and could lead to production relocation.
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: EU Carbon Pricing and Subsidies Drive Green Steel Investments
forces.description: EU carbon pricing under the Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) and the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) are creating a cost advantage for low-emission DRI-EAF steel production over traditional BF-BOF routes. Coupled with heavy subsidies, particularly in Germany and Sweden, these policies are supporting new investments in green steel plants. This policy-driven support is essential for overcoming high production costs in Europe and fostering the transition to decarbonized steel manufacturing.
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: Asian BF-BOF Steel Undercuts European DRI-EAF Costs
forces.description: BF-BOF steel production in Asia, particularly India and China, remains significantly more cost-competitive than European DRI-EAF steel. Indian BF-BOF steel costs are $120 less per ton than Oman's DRI-EAF, and Chinese steel is $15 cheaper, making them the most cost-competitive globally. This creates a severe headwind for European steel producers, whose DRI-EAF costs are substantially higher, highlighting the ongoing challenge in global price competition despite decarbonization efforts.
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: Soaring Global Demand for Energy Transition Materials
forces.description: Global demand for critical minerals like lithium, copper, rare earth elements, nickel, and manganese is experiencing unprecedented growth. This surge is driven by the energy transition, including the proliferation of electric vehicles (EVs), renewable energy infrastructure, and advancements in AI and advanced manufacturing. McKinsey estimates a 4.5% CAGR in demand for energy transition materials through 2035, creating a strong tailwind for the Metals & Mining sector, particularly for producers of these key materials.
forces.source_title: African bedrock: How the continent’s minerals can help power the world

forces.title: Critical Mineral Supply Chains Face Persistent Constraints and Disruptions
forces.description: The global supply of critical materials, including rare earth elements, nickel, and manganese, faces persistent constraints related to ore quality, processing, and infrastructure. These challenges are intensifying due to geopolitical conflicts and rising resource nationalism, which disrupt mineral flows and investor sentiment. For European industries reliant on these imports, this presents a key risk to supply chain security and cost stability, potentially hindering energy and technology transitions.
forces.source_title: African bedrock: How the continent’s minerals can help power the world

forces.title: Resource Nationalism and Local Value-Addition in Critical Minerals
forces.description: There is a growing global trend towards mineral sovereignty and local value-addition in critical minerals, notably reflected in the G20 Critical Minerals Framework. This shifts developing nations from raw exports towards processing and adding value domestically. For European importers, this represents a structural change in supply dynamics, potentially impacting the availability and cost of raw critical minerals, and necessitating adjustments in sourcing strategies to secure supply chains.
forces.source_title: African bedrock: How the continent’s minerals can help power the world

viewpoints.title: Irish Metals Sector Demonstrates Resilience Despite Headwinds and Softening Global Prices
viewpoints.description: The metals sector in Ireland is showing resilience, supported by strong links to construction, engineering, manufacturing, and agri-business. Despite a moderation in construction activity, the sector benefits from ongoing projects. However, it faces challenges from softer global metal prices, persistent raw material and labor cost pressures, and uncertainties from international trade policies and tariffs. Major steel stockholders maintain favorable liquidity, and insolvency levels are low, suggesting a stable but watchful outlook for the sector.

viewpoints.title: Europe's Green Steel Transition Faces High Energy Costs, Needs Policy Support
viewpoints.description: The transition to DRI-EAF and hydrogen-powered DRI-EAF steel manufacturing in Europe, notably in Germany and Sweden, is gaining traction due to environmental reasons and policy support. However, this shift is challenged by structurally higher natural gas and electricity costs, making European DRI-EAF production 45-50% more expensive than in regions like Oman. Viability hinges on continued carbon pricing mechanisms like EU ETS and CBAM, alongside subsidies and a 'green' premium, otherwise it lags behind cheaper BF-BOF production from Asia.
viewpoints.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

demand_drivers.description: EU-27 carbon pricing and the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) increase costs for traditional BF-BOF production, creating a relative advantage and investment incentive for lower-carbon DRI-EAF plants.

market_sizing.methodology: Planned production capacity from more than 17 EAF and DRI-EAF steel plants under development across Europe.
market_sizing.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

demand_drivers.description: The need for lower CO2 emissions is driving demand for DRI-EAF technology, which is a scalable pathway to reduce emissions in steel production.

pnl_drivers.description: High natural gas costs in Europe (e.g., Sweden's prices 4-5x Oman's, Germany's 2-3x Oman's) significantly increase the levelized cost of DRI-EAF steel production, impacting profitability.
Elevated electricity costs, particularly in Germany (nearly double Oman's), add a substantial markup to the per-ton cost of DRI-EAF steel.
EU ETS and CBAM add material CO2 costs, penalizing BF-BOF production and creating a relative advantage for DRI-EAF as allowances phase out, influencing overall cost structures and pricing.
Access to key metallic inputs like DRI-grade iron ore and high-quality scrap is crucial for DRI-EAF economics. Advanced economies benefit from higher scrap availability, reducing material costs.

new_opportunities.description: Switching to hydrogen-powered DRI-EAF could reduce levelized costs (e.g., in Sweden from $750 to $665 per ton), offering a pathway to lower-emission steel and improved competitiveness.

market_sizing.methodology: Analysis of levelized costs for DRI-EAF steel production, benchmarking various geographies against Oman to understand cost drivers.
market_sizing.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

demand_drivers.description: Global efforts towards renewable energy and electrification, including electric vehicles (EVs) and renewable energy infrastructure, are significantly increasing demand for materials like lithium, copper, nickel, manganese, and rare earth elements.
The expansion of artificial intelligence technologies and advanced manufacturing processes requires a steady supply of critical minerals as foundational inputs.

market_sizing.methodology: McKinsey's Global Materials Perspective 2025 estimates demand for energy transition materials. This directly impacts the market for critical minerals and non-ferrous metals.
market_sizing.source_title: African bedrock: How the continent’s minerals can help power the world
